The 1960s were a time of great change in the United States. The country was undergoing a period of rapid economic growth and social upheaval, with many Americans living in poverty.
In response to this new reality, President Lyndon B. Johnson launched the Great Society program that sought to improve the lives of millions of people by providing them with jobs, education, health care, housing, and other services.
This program was designed to help American workers gain skills they could use for their careers. It also helped reduce unemployment rates and increase productivity.
President Johnson’s goal was to create an economy where everyone had access to quality work opportunities. He believed that this would lead to greater prosperity for all Americans.
However, there were some critics who argued that the Great Society programs did not go far enough. They argued that it was too expensive and that government spending on these programs was not sustainable.
Despite these criticisms, President Johnson continued his efforts to promote equality and fairness throughout America. In 1964, he signed into law the Civil Rights Act of 1964 which outlawed discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, or national origin.
